What survives it: the authored-label machinery, the carrier MEASUREMENT ( Heavy is self-defeating — his own damage walls his growth at hit ~13), and the live doctrine that damage-coupled growth is self-limiting. The retirement's own record is the `nocombo-r34` entry below.]**
*The mechanic.* `skill.lenSteps` on a fighter row **adds ladder steps** to the weapon trait's growth: `LEN_CAP[i] = LEN_STEPS + skill.lenSteps`, the ladder is built once per weapon to `LEN_STEPS_TOP` (18), and `grow()` clamps each fighter at their own cap. This is the first real **hook** — r26's comment "no hook machinery" was true of the *rate* (a weapon-row number) and false of the *cap*, which is now fighter data reaching into what the trait can do. Carrier **Speedy**, `lenSteps: 6` → cap 18 = **+420%**, drawn tip **766.631px**, shaft k 7.8760, **89 circles** at the top step. Six new baked rows; rows 1-12 are **byte-identical to r28** by diff, so a non-carrier's geometry is literally unchanged. Legend labels are now **authored** per row (`short`) with a boot guard — the old `spin ? '+SPD' : '+DMG'` derivation would have printed a wrong label for any third axis.
*Sizing was measured, not guessed.* The spear already **saturates the 12-step base in 85% of rounds** (115 rounds, 50 forced-spear cells, mean max step 11.28), so the only headroom a special could use was steps 13-24. Damaging hits per round: median **24**, and 24 is a **lethality wall** rather than a coincidence — base dmg 1 plus the trait's +0.3 per hit crosses 100 hp exactly at hit 24 (cumulative 106.8), so *"no cap let it snowball"* already had a natural stop and any cap above 24 is unreachable by construction. Cap 18 was chosen as reachable in ~75% of rounds and inside the covering feasibility already probed to +400%; the bake then confirmed it (all 18 steps gate-PASS on their own stretched art, poke -0.30px throughout, worst miss **4.35px** of the 4.6 band at step 15).
*The carrier was chosen by measurement and the obvious pick was WRONG.* Heavy was tried first and is **self-defeating**: his own +0.9 dmg per hit makes cumulative damage cross 100 hp at hit ~13, so his spear walls at step 13 — measured **0/68 rounds saturating, median top step 13**. Speedy's damage stays at base, so he lives long enough in the round to grow it out: **median 18, 54/68 (79%) saturating**. The rule this leaves behind: **a length skill belongs on the low-damage cast**, and every future carrier needs the same check, because a fighter's damage growth sets the hit budget the ladder has to fit inside.
*One measurement retracted, one misattribution corrected — both by cross-check rather than by argument.* (a) A hit counter derived from `|f.spin| / 0.30` reported a plausible median but was **unsound**: round 1 always read exactly 36 and later rounds read 0 while the sim's own `lenStep` said 7 and 12. Spin is not monotonic and the per-round base was mis-sampled. It was replaced by lifting the clamp in a scratch copy and reading `f.lenStep` directly — a derived counter must be validated against sim state before it is believed. (b) The r28→r29 differential showed **20/20** forced-spear cells diverging at tick 286, which read as "the skill changes battles". The **non-carrier control** — spear in Heavy's slot, cap 12 in *both* builds, rows 1-12 byte-identical — diverges **10/10 at the same tick with `lenStep 0/0` in both**. The cause is `REACH.spear` rising 505.488 → **829.571**: REACH is a per-**weapon** table feeding the substep budget, so a taller ladder changes the numerics of **every** spear battle, not just the carrier's. Recorded consequences: build-proof section N's claim that "any divergence is the growth itself" was **false** and is corrected, the side effect is now an assertion rather than a footnote, and **no spear cell can be claimed behaviour-identical across a ladder raise**. Measured cost: 0.2590 → **0.3561 ms/tick, +37.5%** on spear battles.
*Proofs (Tier 0+1, since geometry moved):* build-proof **58/58** · `inscribe` exit 0 · `lengrow-bake --verify` **18/18** · leadproof / flipproof / chromecheck PASS · the art never thickens across all 18 steps (the full lateral l-set compared step by step) · `MINR.spear` still **2.00** · fingerprints **0 of 8** for the fourth consecutive build, no twin file written, still blind.
*Arena, flagged not assumed.* REACH 829.571 is **1.66×** the 500px half-arena, so a fully grown carrier spear hangs ~330px past the wall from mid-arena. The owner accepted +200% (505px) on playtest — *"it looks good now"* — but +420% is 1.66× that and is his call on sight, not mine by extrapolation.
*Machinery for the remaining 21 weapons, which is the point of landing it this way.* `LEN_CAP` is computed from the rows, the ladder is built once per weapon to the max cap, and **both the bake tool and the build-proof now loop over growers and fighters instead of naming the spear and Speedy** — so a second carrier is a row edit and a second growing weapon is a row edit plus a re-bake. `lengrow-bake.mjs` gained `--emit FILE` (write the block without touching the canonical, so a code edit and a geometry edit land **atomically** — otherwise the boot guard rejects the file mid-transition) and `--steps N` (probe a taller ladder; refuses `--write`). **Scope kept deliberately narrow:** length is the spear's alone by owner ruling (max weapon length = the spear's), so the tool's one-grower guard stays and fails loudly rather than silently baking one weapon's rows for another. The other weapons' skills — shot multipliers, knock — need **no baking at all**: a row field plus a hook, with no covering to re-pack and no gate to pass.
*Owed:* the deferred bundle is unchanged (484-cell re-run, resolver rework, spear-bearing fingerprint cell — all at the END of the skills pass). New: the carrier is data-decided but the owner may overrule on playtest; law-3's band at REACH 829.571 is unmeasured; and the +37.5% spear-battle sim cost is disclosed but not optimised.

**Two skill seams land ahead of the remaining 21 weapons — `seam-r30`, behaviour-identical, and the readiness finding that made them necessary (2026-10-28; owner, told the code was not yet ready for 22 unique skills: *"build it first, and note it down in the docs and clean the docs and codebase, i wanna start a new chat"*. Canonical md5 `11f87c88b2bb091988fd0c34abdac298` → **`50adefa2aefaa5d8fe1aca1e5c8479cb`**, 3,332 → **3,362 lines**, stamp `skill-r29` → **`seam-r30`**.)**
*The readiness finding.* `grow()` (sim :1703) was the **only** consumer of `skill`/`trait` data in the entire sim, so a "skill" could only ever mean one of three numbers on one trigger ("damaging hit"). Three gaps stood between that and 22 unique skills: **(1)** one trigger only; **(2)** `emit()` is an append-only log, not a bus — nine kinds (bounce, hit ×2, ko, parry, roll, swat, wall, **shotFire**) pushed to `G.events` for VFX and audit, with no subscriber mechanism, so nothing can *react* to a moment; **(3)** knock has no single seam at all — there is no `CFG.knock`, it is applied diffusely at shot landings (:2132), parry shoves and wall bounces, which makes it the expensive one of the three owner-authorized hook targets. **Deliberately NOT built:** a general hook or plugin framework. That is the over-engineering the owner rejects; a seam gets added when a skill needs it.
*Seam A — authored `brief`.* `APP.meta.weapons[].brief` (sim :3237) was derived from the same binary `trait.spin ? '+SPD / Hit' : '+DMG / Hit'` test that `skill-r29` had just removed from `SKILL_SHORT` — a second site of the same class, missed at the time. And it was **already wrong**: the spear's trait is length growth, and its exported brief read `'+DMG / Hit'` with no mention of growing. Now an authored `brief` on the row wins, the derivation survives as a fallback for plain spin/dmg rows (so this cost no 22-row churn), and a boot guard **throws** if a row carries a trait axis outside `{spin, dmg}` with no authored brief. The spear ships `'+DMG +LEN / Hit'`, matching the fighter-row `short` convention.
*Seam B — shot cadence.* `shot.mult` on the weapon row and `skill.shotMult` on the fighter **add** (owner ruling: stacking adds), and the effective value divides the launch accumulator's `need`, so 2 fires the same volley twice as often. Cadence rather than extra projectiles per release, because `shot.revs` already owns "how much spin per volley" and `shot.volley` already owns the fan — a third way to mean "more shots" would be one too many. A boot guard rejects a non-positive effective multiplier for **every (weapon, fighter) pair**, since the release loop divides by it and would otherwise hang. **No row declares it yet**: the seam ships inert, which is exactly why the landing is behaviour-identical.
*Measured, because an inert seam is indistinguishable from dead code.* New **`.qa/seam-proof.mjs`** (**8/8**, Tier 0, ~2s) assigns a synthetic `shot.mult` and counts throws over 3000 ticks of bow-vs-hammer: **13 → 28 → 92** for mult 0 → 1 → 3. It also reports the **superlinearity**: 2.15× realised for a declared 2×, ~7× for a declared 4×, because more shots → more damaging hits → more spin growth → more shots. Any future carrier must be sized on the realised factor, not the declared one. Both guards are proven to **FIRE** by injecting a bad row into the extracted source and requiring the boot error — a guard that never throws reads as coverage and is worse than no guard. Rest of Tier 0: build-proof **58/58** unchanged, chromecheck PASS (legend 812B), fingerprints **0 of 8** and meaningful for the first time in five builds.
*A correction, disclosed before it entered the record.* I told the owner the shot launch loop "emits nothing at all". It emits `shotFire` at both the volley and single-shot paths, with `by/sid/x/y/dmg/fx/fy/fAng`; my grep pattern `[a-z0-9]*` had missed the capital F, so I reported 8 event kinds instead of 9 and drew the wrong conclusion about the launch site. The "not a subscribable bus" half of the assessment stands and is what Seam B works around.
*Owed:* unique skills for the remaining **21 weapons**, each now a row field plus one consumer site plus one assertion — the `lenSteps` pattern, not a per-weapon investigation · **knock** needs a decision about *which* knock (shot landing, parry shove, wall bounce) before it can be a seam at all · a **second trigger** only when a skill needs one, never speculatively · more bots, after the weapons · the deferred bundle unchanged (484-cell re-run, resolver rework, spear fingerprint cell — all at the END of the skills pass).

**The pairing step — a match can now pick 2 of N cast members. `pair-r31`, behaviour-identical on the shipped pairing (2026-10-28; owner, after the assistant recommended building it ahead of more bots: *"go"*. Canonical md5 `18096bdbf0f5cb80d33a8d32cee86609` → **`5a2ce808ad92097f6389b516075f0a68`**, 3,410 → **3,446 lines**, stamp `seam-r30` → **`pair-r31`**.)**

*What changed.* `newGame(seed, { cast: [i, j] })` picks which two cast members play and on which side; `DEFAULT_CAST = [0, 1]` is the shipped pairing, so every battle so far is the default and the landing is behaviour-identical by construction. The mechanism is a **field split**: `f.idx` is the CAST IDENTITY (the row in `FIGHTERS`) and `f.slot` is the SIDE (0 = the left spawn, 1 = the right). They were one field, and 28 sites now read `slot` where they mean left/right while 7 keep reading `idx` where they mean *who*. Slot-keyed: `SPAWN`, the roll order `w0`/`w1`, the launch direction sign, `wins`/`winner`/`roundWinner`, `1 - f.slot`, `view`/`flashV`/`flipAnim`/`koStill.pose`, the `C0`/`C1` circle scratch, `fs[st.o]`, and every event actor ref (`by`/`to`/`o`/`winner`/`loser`). Idx-keyed: `COLS`, `TINTS`, `LEN_CAP`, `SKILL_SHORT`, `FIGHTERS[idx].skill`, `meta.fighters`. **`G.cast[slot]` is the only map between them.** Guarded at boot *and* on every construction (wrong length, out-of-range, non-integer and non-array all throw; `null`/`undefined` mean "the default", which is what the lever relies on). `APP.setCast([i, j])` is the console lever — no UI chip, deliberately, while the cast is two; it persists across seed changes, so the pairing is a session choice and the seed is per-battle.

*The crux, which is why this was not a nine-site rename.* One field was already being read **both ways**: the `hit` event's `to` fed `flashV[e.to]` (an identity-coloured flash, idx-keyed) *and* `koStill.pose[e.to]` (a slot-keyed array, because `view[i]` is built by iterating `fighters[i]`). Those coincide only while idx === slot, so a swapped pairing would have aliased two actors into one scratch entry — the kill still would have frozen the wrong body. The same ambiguity sat on `st.o`, which is read as `fs[st.o]` in `shotHitBody` *and* as `fs[1 - st.o]` in `shotStep` *and* as `G.fighters[st.o]` in the copy-weapon draw. The rule adopted and documented in `newFighter`: **event actor refs carry SLOTS**, because every consumer of them is a slot-keyed array (`measure.mjs` included — it indexes `curW = [e.w0, e.w1]` with `e.by`). A cast identity in an event is recoverable as `G.cast[slot]`; the reverse is not.

*Measured.* New **`.qa/pair-proof.mjs`** (**31/31**, Tier 0, ~25s) runs pairings where slot ≠ idx — the half the fingerprint suite cannot see, since it only ever plays the default. It sweeps **103,076 ticks** across 14 battles (10 natural-roll + 4 forced-mirror that really finish, so the `ko`/`winner` path is not vacuous: 285 hits, 10 K.O.s, 4/4 decided) and asserts the foe invariant `fs[f.slot] === f && fs[1 - f.slot] !== f` every tick, that every event actor ref is a slot with `to === 1 - by`, that `st.o` indexes `fs`, that each fighter wears the weapon its SLOT was rolled, and that rule 6's counter-rotation holds per side. **The decisive number:** with forced mirror hammers the weapon trait is identical on both sides, so damage-per-hit isolates the actor's skill — it measures exactly **0.70/hit on Speedy's slot and 1.60/hit on Heavy's** (hammer `trait.dmg` 0.7 + skill 0.0 / 0.9), and under `cast: [1, 0]` those two rates **exchange sides**. The skill travels with the actor. Same seed, swapped pairing: 13,767 ticks, wins 0–2, winner slot 1 → 17,770 ticks, wins 2–1, winner slot 0. A **mirror pairing `[0, 0]` is legal** and fights to a decision (14,157 ticks, 2–0), which matters because nothing may key the foe lookup off `idx`. `chromecheck.mjs` grew a **pairing section** (still PASS, ~26s) covering the one surface `pair-proof` cannot see: under `setCast([1, 0])` the scorebug names exchange (`Speedy / Heavy` → `Heavy / Speedy`), the identity swatches exchange with them (`#a8892f #ff6b4a` → `#ff6b4a #a8892f`, so colour travels with the actor and not with the side), the legend rows exchange, the slot-keyed score stays put, the winner overlay names the ACTOR (`"Heavy"` = `cast[0]`), and `setCast(null)` restores the default. Rest of Tier 0/1: build-proof **58/58**, seam-proof **8/8**, bake `--verify` **18/18**, inscribe GATE PASS, leadproof PASS (354 hits / 424 parries / 100 swats recomputed from the stored event fields — which is independent evidence the slot-keyed `by`/`to` are self-consistent), flipproof PASS.

*Fingerprints: 8/8, 0 of 8 diverged — the sixth consecutive, and meaningful for exactly one half of the change.* The suite runs the default pairing, where `slot` and `idx` hold the same number, so 8/8 is real evidence that **the shipped pairing did not move** (the change is inert by construction, and the cells do cover shots, kills and the wins path). It is **silent by construction on the swapped pairing** — no fingerprint cell can ever exercise it, which is the whole reason `pair-proof` exists. `measure.mjs` stays valid untouched for the same reason: it reads `FIGHTERS[G.winner]` and `curW[e.by]`, both correct while `cast` is `[0, 1]`. **Recorded as an assumption, not a fix:** `measure.mjs` therefore reports the default pairing only, and would misname winners under any other; it is owner-gated and no other pairing has ever been run through it.

*Owed:* the cast is still two — **more bots need an owner-chosen colour each** (`COLS`/`TINTS` hold exactly two entries, as do `SPAWN`, `view`, `flashV`, `flipAnim` and `C0`/`C1`), so a third bot is a row + a colour + a two-entry-array widening, not a structural change · no cast-selection UI (the console lever is deliberate while N = 2; a picker is a chrome design question) · a 3-way brawl remains structural · the deferred bundle is unchanged (484-cell re-run, resolver rework, spear fingerprint cell — all at the END of the skills pass).

**Whole-file code-review cleanup #5 — and the `pair-r31` renderer bug it caught. `review-r32` (2026-10-28, owner order: *"Review spinclash preview.html for bugs, code smells, dead/unused code, duplicate or redundant logic, unnecessary complexity, unused imports/references, and potential performance issues, remove unused code. Refactor and consolidate where appropriate, simplify the implementation, improve readability and maintainability, optimize inefficient code, and fix any issues found without changing the intended behavior. Read the docs and see if they align with everything also, and trim old text or sections we no longer need."* Canonical md5 `5a2ce808ad92097f6389b516075f0a68` → **`77eaf6b2eb2cfa4a8ae36200bc92a35d`**, 3,446 → **3,457 lines**, stamp `pair-r31` → **`review-r32`**.)**

*The bug — one landing old, and three proofs walked past it.* `pair-r31` split `f.slot` (side) from `f.idx` (cast identity) and converted 28 sites. It missed the **renderer's cast-table reads**: the VS-poster reveal indexes `COLS[i]`, `TINTS[i]` and `FIGHTERS[i]` by `i`, the poster *half*, and `drawShot`/`drawCastFlash` index `COLS[st.o]` by the shot's owner — and both `i` and `st.o` are **slots**, while `COLS`/`TINTS`/`FIGHTERS` are **cast**-keyed. Thirteen sites. Under `DEFAULT_CAST = [0, 1]` the two coincide, so the shipped game is correct and nothing observable was wrong; call `APP.setCast([1, 0])` and the reveal poster names, colours and describes the **wrong bot on each half** — Speedy's name, gold disc and skill prose over the side Heavy actually fights from. **Why nothing caught it:** fingerprints hash *sim state* and only ever play the default pairing; chromecheck's default section reads the scorebug and legend (which `pair-r31` did convert correctly); `pair-proof` sections A–H are sim-level and never look at a canvas. The class is *renderer reads of a cast table keyed by a slot*, and every existing instrument was blind to it by construction.

*The fix, and the proof that the fix is not decorative.* All thirteen reads now go through `G.cast` — `vsHalf` and the poster loop take a documented `const ci = G.cast[i]` local, and the shot sigils read `COLS[G.cast[st.o]]`. `pair-proof.mjs` grew **section I**, which loads block 1 against a **recording canvas stub** (capturing `fillStyle`/`fillText` with coordinates, `measureText` returning a real width so the poster takes its measured centring branch), captures `requestAnimationFrame` and hand-steps the real frame loop 120 frames into the reveal at a fixed seed. It asserts the left half's name is `FIGHTERS[G.cast[0]].name` and the right's `G.cast[1]` — default reads SPEEDY/HEAVY, `[1, 0]` reads HEAVY/SPEEDY — that the skill prose travels with the same actor, and it adds a **comment-aware static tripwire**: a string-and-comment-stripping scanner audits all **23** code reads of `COLS`/`TINTS`/`FIGHTERS`/`SKILL_SHORT`/`LEN_CAP` and requires every index to be an identity (`…idx`, `…cast…`, the poster's `ci`, or the roster build's own `FIGHTERS.map((f, i) => …)`). **Proven to fire, per the house rule:** run against the pre-fix `pair-r31` canonical, section I reports **4 FAILs** and the tripwire names all thirteen offending sites by line. `pair-proof` is now **37/37**.

*Dead code, duplication and the correction to cleanup #4's scan.* **Removed:** `const rect = (d0, d1, l0, l1) => …` (canonical :220), an art helper from the original weapon-authoring trio `rect`/`star`/`build` that no row calls — `star` and `build` are both live. **This falsifies cleanup #4's headline claim** that "all 383 top-level declarations were scanned… exactly ONE has none — `geom`". `geom` *is* load-bearing and stays; but the scan that cleared `rect` counted bare tokens, and `rect` has four look-alikes that are not references to it (`g.rect(…)`, two `ctx.rect(…)`, and the CSS `clip: rect(0,0,0,0)` in `.sr-only`). A strict scan — word-bounded and excluding property access — leaves only the declaration. **Recorded so the next scan does not repeat it: token-counting a short identifier that is also a canvas method name and a CSS function will always produce a false "referenced".** **Consolidated:** the reveal/fight branch in `draw()` opened with a *byte-identical* `for (const f of G.fighters) drawBody(f, view[f.slot].x, view[f.slot].y);` in both arms; bodies draw first in every phase, so the loop is hoisted above the branch and each arm keeps only its own layer. Draw order is unchanged (bodies, then poster **or** weapons + shots), and the weapon arm now takes one `const v = view[f.slot]` local instead of five property chains. Cleanup #4's normalised 3-line-window scan had missed this because the two copies are separated by `drawReveal()` / the branch line rather than being adjacent.

*Audited and found clean — recorded so the next pass does not redo it.* All **34** `CFG` keys are read. No weapon-row field is unread (the full read set is `brief, chain, chainTie, dmg, headLead, hold, lead, len, lenJ, line, name, omega, poly, shot, trait, tuck`). No dead CSS selectors (19 classes, all with consumers). No `console.*`, no `debugger`, no TODO/FIXME, no loose `==` outside the four idiomatic `!= null` guards (which are *correct* — `st.o` can legitimately be `0`, so a truthiness test would drop slot 0). The per-substep hot path (`stepPhysics` → `bladeVsBlade` → `fireShots` → `shotStep`) allocates nothing but event payloads, and `bladeCircles` still writes into a caller-supplied array. **Deliberately NOT consolidated:** `bladeVsBody`'s damage block and `shotHitBody` look like duplicates and are not — they knock along different axes (the body line vs the shot's flight line), emit different payloads (attacker pose fields vs shot fields), only the blade path carries the `W.shot || hold === 'tangential'` gate, and `measure.mjs`'s law-4 replica mirrors that gate exactly. Merging them would buy ten lines and cost a branch-heavy signature over two different physical events.

*Deliberately NOT removed.* `APP.setShotArt`, `APP.setAccent` and `APP.shotArtOf` have **zero callers** in the file and zero in any harness — their consumer was the arena review bench, retired at the 2026-10-28 checkpoint clean. They are kept because the **kit-route rebuild is owed** and that bench is its judge; deleting the hooks would make the rebuild re-derive them. Flagged here rather than silently kept. Also kept, extending #3/#4's lists: `geom` (the harness export surface) · `W.chainTie.worstI` (the diagnostic a red chain-tie gate needs) · `info().flipT` (flipproof reads it) · the orb's `tuck: false` (a documented no-op clip, kept in case its art grows inward) · the four largest functions · `drawPolySet`'s eleven positional parameters (an options object would allocate in the draw path).

*Perf — one boundary worth stating, because "optimize inefficient code" has a hard limit here.* **No sim arithmetic was touched, and none should be.** Replacing `Math.hypot` with `Math.sqrt(dx*dx + dy*dy)`, reassociating a sum, or hoisting a multiplication out of a loop can all change the last ulp, and the sim is fingerprint-load-bearing: a one-ulp drift diverges a battle within ticks and invalidates the standing baseline. The only legitimate optimisations are ones that cannot change a float result — avoiding allocation, caching a lookup, removing dead work — and the allocation scan says there is nothing left to win. The measured cost of the one thing that *did* move geometry this pass (`skill-r29`'s taller ladder) is already disclosed at +37.5% ms/tick on spear battles.

**Bind fix — `bindfix-r35`: latched binds push apart from their first tick, and crossed weapons rotate open instead of freezing (2026-10-31; owner playtest, seed 32542 crossbow×staff: *"the crossbow and staff is basically locked up together for a few seconds, this looks very ugly and bad, and should not be possible"*, diagnosis accepted, fix scope C approved. Canonical md5 `7c51200b05929a7231ea126bd35df84c` → **`a1cb90eb2a017d68e33cbf7a4131ef69`**, 3,507 → **3,525 lines**, stamp `nocombo-r34` → **`bindfix-r35`**.)**
*Diagnosis — reproduced headless at the same seed (two 74–75-tick binds back-to-back in round 1), then traced tick by tick.* Two mechanisms losing a force battle in the worst-case geometry, not one bug. (1) The clinch spring's smoothstep ramp (`2200·sm`) only overtakes the press that holds a vertical/rim stack at clinchT ≈ 31 of 48 — for the first ~25 ticks of such a bind the spring loses and the pair reads as a dead lock (bodies clamped at exactly 2·bodyR, speeds ~0). (2) The pin-escape nudge's live torque sign sawtooths in a symmetric X-cross — crossbow bow-arms × a shaft: the deepest contacting circle pair alternates sides tick to tick, measured ±0.046 rad/tick against a spin·dt of 0.046, net rotation ZERO — so the crossed weapons visibly freeze and vibrate instead of orbiting out. Launcher×launcher shows it worst: spine damage is zero by the projectile rule, so no hit recoil or kill ever breaks the pose. Pre-fix frequency: 2/12 forced crossbow+staff cells and 2/20 naturals, 54–75 ticks each.
*The fix — two dials inside the existing seams, stateless.* `CFG.clinchFloor` 1500: while the blade latch is shut the separation acceleration is floored, so a bind pushes itself apart from its FIRST tick; mature binds (sm→1 ⇒ 2200) and the post-release decay are untouched — a force, never an impulse, doctrine intact. And inside a latched bind the pin-escape nudge takes the sign of each weapon's own spin (rotate WITH the orbit, up to twice the orbit rate opens the scissors) instead of the live torque sign; unlatched deep wedges keep the physical torque sign. The first design — latch the torque sign once per episode — was measured and DROPPED: a captured wrong scissor direction held one bind for 384 ticks.
*Chosen by a four-variant sweep, same 32 cells (12 forced crossbow+staff + 20 naturals).* none: 4 binds incl. the owner's seed · floor alone: owner seed cleared but 247/596/384-tick open-space cross-tracking monsters appeared (bodies pushed apart while long weapons keep crossing) · floor + torque-latched nudge: monsters partly remain · **floor + spin-aligned nudge (shipped): 1/12 forced (64t, sawtooth-free) + 2/20 naturals (48t clean; 69t an axe×flail chain wrap — a different texture, pre-existing, and its tail separates textbook-clean: full ramp, d opening ~15px/tick)**. Owner seed and s99 clean; every monster dead.

## Testing recipe (headless)

**Owner ruling 2026-10-28 — the proof battery is TIERED, not per-landing.** Owner, with more skills and bots queued: *"i really dont think all this testing is nescessary, we are adding a lot more skills and bots, so if you do this each time its going to take forever."* He is right, and the cause was habit: most of the battery exists because the length-growth builds re-baked geometry, which a shot-multiplier or knock skill does not. So, in force from `skill-r29` onwards — **Tier 0, every landing (~1 min):** a boot probe (does it load, do the numbers read right, does the hook actually fire) plus `.qa/lengrow-build-proof.mjs`, plus `chromecheck` only if a label or legend changed. **Tier 1, only if geometry moved** (art, polys, coverings, scale): `inscribe.mjs`, `lengrow-bake --verify`, `leadproof`, `flipproof`. **Tier 2, only on suspicion or once at the end of the pass:** differential sweeps, cost measurements, fingerprints. Measured-facts entries get correspondingly **shorter** — what changed, the numbers that matter, what is owed — not fifteen sub-points. What is *not* cut: a measurement that can **change a decision**. The carrier choice for the first special skill was settled by five minutes of measurement that falsified the obvious pick (Heavy is self-defeating; see the `skill-r29` entry), which is design work rather than verification, and it stays.

The harness conventions carried over from the abandoned project — they caught every real bug there, and two here on day one (the stall tail, the missing buzzsaw). All harnesses drive `spinclash-preview.html` (canonical filename — harnesses default to it).

**STANDING RULE (owner, 2026-10-19): `measure.mjs` NEVER runs without the owner's explicit go — "dont run measure.mjs. (atleast not untill i say so, ever. ask if you want to)."** Ask first; use the fast probe for iteration. **The rule was exercised 2026-10-28:** the owner asked for the run, then ran Parts 0-4 himself on his own Windows machine while the sandbox took Parts 5-6. **Split-baseline procedure, now proven end to end:** `--cells a+b,c+d --matrix-only` skips naturals and determinism, and the parts' battle sets are disjoint so the law counters sum exactly; cut the 484 cells from the roster the harness itself prints (`--vs nosuchweapon` exits 2 and lists all 22), keep each command well inside cmd.exe's 8,191-character limit (81 cells is about 1.2 KB), give every part its own output file, and aggregate with `scratch/measure-agg.mjs` (read-only — sums counters, maxes extremes, re-derives winner splits, and asserts the parts share no cell). **Redirect with `>`: the harness writes no files of its own**, there is not one write call in it — re-verified 2026-10-28 after the attribution patch: **0 write calls at 1,216 lines**. On Windows use cmd.exe — Git Bash's `tee` died with the VS Code terminal (`stdout is not a tty`) and PowerShell converts the harness's stderr progress ticker into `NativeCommandError` text that looks like a crash. Cost: 26-73 min per 81-cell part at 8 workers, 124 min for a 79-cell part at 2; two workers measured no faster in aggregate than one on a 2-core box, so `--jobs` buys nothing there. Harness md5 `3ba90d73a502bcef6313111546740d30` since the law-3 field fix. Matrix-scale baselines belong on the owner's machine as one command (minutes there), or in owner-sanctioned `--matrix-only` chunks.

It exists because the standing fingerprint suite **cannot** cover this mechanism: fingerprints play `DEFAULT_CAST`, where `f.slot === f.idx`, so a slot/idx mix-up is invisible to them by construction. It runs pairings where they differ (`[1, 0]` and the mirror `[0, 0]`), sweeps the foe invariant `fs[f.slot] === f && fs[1 - f.slot] !== f` every tick, checks that every event actor ref is a slot with `to === 1 - by` and that `st.o` indexes `fs`, and **asserts its own sample sizes** so a future stall fails loudly instead of passing on zero observations (the house vacuity rule). # ARENA ENGINE

A localhost-only Node.js tool that turns a seeded game configuration into a finished MP4.

```
pick a game → set options → generate → watch it → download
```

No cloud, no accounts, no telemetry, no network calls after `npm install`. Binds `127.0.0.1` and writes files to `output/`.

**The purpose:** those MP4s get published to ad-supported platforms — YouTube, TikTok, Reels — and earn from the ads on them. The video file is the product; everything else in this repo is scaffolding to produce it. See the Purpose section at the top of `SPEC.md` before making any tradeoff.

**Requirements:** Node 22+, VSCode. ffmpeg, the canvas runtime and the fonts all arrive with `npm install`.

---

## Read these

| | |
|---|---|
| **[GAMES.md](./GAMES.md)** | **Read first.** Game design state: what exists, open questions, measured facts, test recipe. |
| [SPEC.md](./SPEC.md) | The rules. Architecture, stack, pipeline, output specs, video-quality requirements, house style, studio UX, repo layout, what must never be introduced. |
| **[CONTRACT.md](./CONTRACT.md)** | The interface a game implements. Services injected, what a game may not do, timeline shape, the eight compliance checks. |
| **[BUILD.md](./BUILD.md)** | What to build next. Nine phases with pass/fail gates, the definition of done, and the full quality checklists. |

If you are an AI assistant working on this project: read all four before writing code, and treat SPEC.md's rules as overriding any reasonable default you would otherwise choose.

---

**The slot/idx split is the thing to internalise before touching a fighter.** `f.slot` is the SIDE
(0 = the left spawn, 1 = the right); `f.idx` is the CAST IDENTITY (the row in `FIGHTERS`);
**`G.cast[slot]` is the only map between them.** Slot-keyed: `SPAWN`, the roll order, the direction
sign, `wins`/`winner`, `1 - f.slot`, `view`/`flashV`/`flipAnim`/`koStill.pose`, `C0`/`C1`, `fs[st.o]`
and **every event actor ref** (`by`/`to`/`o`/`winner`/`loser`). Idx-keyed: `COLS`, `TINTS`,
`SKILL_SHORT`, `FIGHTERS[idx].skill`, `meta.fighters` — **including in the renderer**,
which is where `pair-r31` got it wrong: the poster loop's `i` is the *half* (a slot) and `st.o` is a
slot, so every cast-table read there must go through `G.cast`. They hold the same number under
`DEFAULT_CAST = [0, 1]`, which is why the landing looked behaviour-identical — **and why the
fingerprint suite can never check any of it.** Run `.qa/pair-proof.mjs` (sections E, F and **I**)
after any edit near those fields; section I drives the real frame loop against a recording canvas
and statically audits all 27 cast-table reads in the file (`LEN_CAP` left the audited list at
`nocombo-r34` with the table itself).

**More bots is now cheaper, but not free.** The pairing step removed the sim's 1v1 *identity*
assumptions; it did not remove its 1v1 *sizing*. A third bot is a `FIGHTERS` row + **an owner-chosen
colour** + widening the seven arrays that hold exactly two entries (`SPAWN`, `COLS`, `TINTS`, `VIEW`,
`flashV`, `flipAnim`, `C0`/`C1`) — `SKILL_SHORT` already `.map`s over `FIGHTERS`. A
3-way brawl is still structural. There is **no cast-selection UI**: `APP.setCast([i, j])` is a
console lever by design while N = 2, and it persists across seed changes.

## Adding a weapon trait (or a fighter skill) — the recipe

The full axis list, consumer sites and guards live **in the canonical**, in the `TRAIT / SKILL
REGISTRY` comment block immediately above `const WEAPONS = {`. Read that first — it is keyed to
symbol names, not line numbers, so it cannot rot. This is the process around it.

**Step 0 — which cost class?** A trait that is a *number read at an existing site* is **CHEAP**
(minutes). A trait that moves *geometry* (drawn art or a covering) is **EXPENSIVE** (days), because
it needs per-step coverings re-baked through `.qa/lengrow-bake.mjs` with every row gated against its
own stretched art. Only the spear's `len` is in the expensive class so far. If your trait is
expensive, **stop and say so before starting** — that is a conversation, not a task.

**Cheap-class steps.** (1) add the field to the weapon row (`trait.*` / `shot.*`) or the fighter row
(`skill.*`) · (2) add **ONE** consumer line at the site that already handles that moment; if no site
handles it, that is a new seam — add it *there*, do not build a framework · (3) add a boot guard if
the value could break something silently (a division, an index past the baked rows, an unauthored
label) · (4) author `brief` (weapon) / `short` (fighter) if the new axis is not plain spin/dmg — the
derivation cannot express it and the guard will throw · (5) add an assertion to `.qa/seam-proof.mjs`,
**including one that proves the guard FIRES** by injecting a bad row · (6) update the REGISTRY block.

**Proofs — Tier 0 only unless geometry moved.** `.qa/seam-proof.mjs` (~2s) then
`.qa/lengrow-build-proof.mjs` (~60s); `chromecheck` if a label changed; `fingerprint.mjs` if the
landing is *meant* to be behaviour-identical (an inert seam, a comment) — where 0 of 8 IS meaningful.
Tier 1 (`inscribe`, `bake --verify`, `leadproof`, `flipproof`) only if art, polys, coverings or scale
moved. Tier 2 (differential sweeps, cost, the 484-cell run) only on suspicion, or once at the end of
the pass.

**Traps that have already bitten, so you do not repeat them.** A *derived* label silently prints the
WRONG text for any axis the derivation does not know — it did, for the spear, for a whole build. A
declared multiplier is not the realised one: `shot.mult` 2 realises as 2.15× and 4 as ~7×, because
more shots → more hits → more spin growth → more shots. A boot guard never proven to throw reads as
coverage and is worse than none. `emit()` looks like an event bus and is not — it is an append-only
log with no subscribers. **One field was being read two ways**, and only a non-default pairing could
show it: the `hit` event's `to` fed `flashV[e.to]` (identity-coloured) *and* `koStill.pose[e.to]`
(slot-keyed, because `view[i]` is built by iterating `fighters[i]`) — identical while `idx === slot`,
aliasing two actors into one scratch entry the moment they differ. The same ambiguity sat on `st.o`,
read as `fs[st.o]`, `fs[1 - st.o]` and `G.fighters[st.o]` in three different places. **The rule that
came out of it: event actor refs carry SLOTS**, because every consumer is a slot-keyed array
(`measure.mjs` indexes `curW = [e.w0, e.w1]` with `e.by`); a cast identity is recoverable as
`G.cast[slot]` and the reverse is not. **And the general trap: a mechanism that ships inert under its
default is invisible to every standing suite that plays that default** — it needs a probe that runs
it non-default, or the suite keeps reporting a pass it is not entitled to. That trap fired for real
one landing later: `pair-r31` converted the sim's slot sites and **stopped at the renderer**, so the
VS poster and the shot sigils still read `COLS[i]` / `TINTS[i]` / `FIGHTERS[i]` / `COLS[st.o]` by
slot — 13 sites, all correct under `[0, 1]`, all wrong under `[1, 0]`, and invisible to fingerprints
(sim state only), to chromecheck's default section, and to a sim-level pair-proof alike. **The rule:
a slot/idx split has to be audited in the renderer too, and the audit has to drive a canvas.**
**Second lesson, about scanning itself:** cleanup #4 recorded that "exactly ONE top-level
declaration has no in-file reference". Wrong — `rect` (an art helper) has none either, and the scan
that cleared it counted bare tokens, so `g.rect(…)`, two `ctx.rect(…)` and the CSS `clip: rect(…)`
all read as references. **Token-counting a short identifier that is also a canvas method name and a
CSS function always yields a false "referenced"**; scan word-bounded and excluding property access,
and strip comments and strings before auditing reads.

## Adding a bot — the recipe (rewritten by `pair-r31`)

Before the pairing step this was a structural change; it is now a row edit plus a colour. **The
sim's identity assumptions are gone** — nothing left reads `1 - x.idx`, and `SKILL_SHORT`
already `.map`s over `FIGHTERS` (`LEN_CAP` was retired with `lenSteps` at `nocombo-r34`). What remains is *sizing*: seven arrays hold exactly two entries.

**The renderer is part of this, not an afterthought** — that is exactly where `pair-r31` left 13
slot-keyed reads of cast tables, and a third bot makes every one of them observable.

(1) add the `FIGHTERS` row — `id`, `name`, `skill` (the axes it owns), **`short`** (the authored
legend label; a boot guard throws without it), `line` · (2) **ask the owner for its colour** — a raw
cast fill for `COLS` and a ≥4.5:1 deep tint for `TINTS`; the six-colour frame economy is his call,
not the assistant's · (3) widen `COLS`, `TINTS`, `SPAWN`, `VIEW`, `flashV`, `flipAnim` and `C0`/`C1`
from two entries to N — `C0`/`C1` should become one array-of-buffers indexed by slot, since they are
the scratch the parry resolver and the hitbox overlay share · (4) pick the pairing, either
`DEFAULT_CAST` or `APP.setCast([i, j])` · (5) run `.qa/pair-proof.mjs` — it sweeps the foe invariant
and every event actor ref over pairings where `slot ≠ idx`, shows a new bot's skill travelling with
it via the damage-per-hit check, and its **section I** proves the VS poster names and colours the
actor rather than the half. With three cast members, also drive `APP.setCast` over all six ordered
pairings and eyeball the poster each time.

**Do not** add a cast-selection UI while N = 2 (the console lever is deliberate), and **do not**
widen those arrays speculatively for a bot that has not been chosen — the owner is allergic to
over-engineering, and step (2) is a conversation that has to happen first anyway.

---

**Stamp discipline.** A *visible* landing bumps the build stamp; a behaviour-identical one does not.
The REGISTRY block landed under `seam-r30` for that reason — comments are not visible, and
fingerprints confirmed 0 of 8. **Clarified 2026-10-28 by `pair-r31`, which is behaviour-identical
(fingerprints 0 of 8) and DID bump the stamp:** "visible" means *observable by the owner*, not
"changes a pixel on load". `pair-r31` adds `APP.setCast([i, j])`, which he can call and watch the
fighters change sides, so a stamp reading `seam-r30` on a file that has the lever would mislead him
at the console. A comment-only or metadata-only landing still does not bump.

- The owner **plays the preview personally** and reports symptoms. Reproduce headlessly with the measurement harness before patching.

Budget for that, or rebuild the probe, before touching shot behaviour.**
- Allergic to over-engineering. Any mechanism must earn its place; expect "is this actually necessary?" and answer it honestly.

# ARENA ENGINE — Spec

A localhost-only Node.js tool: pick a game → set options → generate → watch it → download the MP4.

Read this with `CONTRACT.md` (the game interface) and `BUILD.md` (what to build next).

---

## Purpose — read this before anything else

This tool exists to produce one thing: **a video that gets published to ad-supported platforms** — YouTube, TikTok, Instagram Reels — and earns money from the ads placed on it.

Ad revenue follows watch time. A video earns when people watch it, keep watching it, and come back for more. That single fact explains almost every rule in this document.

**The video file is the product.** Everything else here — the contract, the server, the studio, the CLI — is scaffolding whose only job is to produce that file. No feature justifies itself by being elegant, general-purpose, or convenient. It justifies itself by making the video better, or by making a video faster to produce without making it worse.

Five consequences to hold onto when making tradeoffs:

1. **Output quality outranks everything.** A technically flawed video — stuttery, banded, illegible, quiet, wrong colorspace — costs revenue directly and cannot be fixed after the fact. Nothing in the codebase is more important than the file that comes out.
2. **Platform compliance is revenue, not pedantry.** Resolution, framerate, codec, loudness, duration and safe zones decide whether a video is eligible and how it's treated. These are hard requirements, not preferences.
3. **Consistent house style is a growth mechanism.** Recognisable videos convert a one-off viewer into a subscriber, and subscribers are what turn watch time into compounding watch time. Ten unrelated-looking games is ten times worse than one channel.
4. **"Works on my machine" is failure.** The bar is: published, watched by a stranger on a phone, monetized. A video is not done when it renders — it's done when it would survive being uploaded.
5. **The tool never touches publishing, accounts or revenue.** It makes the file; a human uploads it. Don't build upload automation, analytics, scheduling or account features — they are permanently out of scope, both because platforms prohibit them and because they distract from the only thing that matters.

---

## Rules that override everything else

1. **Localhost only.** Bind `127.0.0.1`; abort at startup if the resolved bind address isn't loopback. No CORS. Static serving restricted to `apps/studio/dist` and `output/`. No auth, no telemetry, no runtime network calls.
2. **Zero system dependencies.** `npm install` is the entire setup. ffmpeg from `ffmpeg-static`, canvas from `@napi-rs/canvas`, fonts committed to `assets/fonts/`.
3. **Deterministic.** Same game + config + seed = byte-identical MP4. No `Math.random`, `Date.now`, `performance.now`, env or fs reads in `packages/core` or `games/`. Seeded PRNG (sfc32) with `fork(label)` per subsystem. Tested by SHA-256.
4. **Sim and render are separate layers.** Sim never draws; renderer never decides outcomes. `render()` receives a snapshot, not the game instance, so it *cannot* advance state.
5. **`packages/core` is pure TypeScript.** No `node:`, no DOM, no I/O. Enforced by ESLint.
6. **The platform knows nothing about any game.** Zero `gameId` conditionals in platform code, ever. All mechanics and visuals live in `games/<id>/`.
7. **Render offline, frame by frame.** Never capture in real time. Frame N is drawn, handed to ffmpeg, then N+1 begins. A slow frame delays the render; it can never drop out of the video.
8. **One render → any shape.** Aspect ratio is chosen afterwards. 9:16 and 16:9 are two encodes of one timeline, never two simulations.
9. **Design system = canvas drawing functions**, injected as services. Not CSS. Anything styled in CSS cannot appear in a video frame.
10. **One render job at a time.** No queue, no parallelism, no batch mode.
11. **CLI parity.** Everything the studio does, `npm run generate` does headless.

---

## Stack

| | |
|---|---|
| Runtime | Node 22, ESM, TypeScript 5 `strict` |
| Monorepo | npm workspaces: `packages/core`, `packages/render`, `packages/server`, `apps/studio` |
| Raster | `@napi-rs/canvas` (Skia, prebuilt, deterministic) |
| Encode | `ffmpeg-static` + `child_process` spawn. Fallback: `ARENA_FFMPEG` env → PATH |
| Schema | Zod — one schema drives validation, defaults, UI panel and CLI flags |
| Server | Fastify + `@fastify/static` |
| UI | Vite + React 18 + Zustand + plain CSS custom properties |
| Dev/test | tsx, Vitest, concurrently, ESLint, Prettier |

**Never introduce:** Playwright/Puppeteer, Remotion, Electron/Tauri, ffmpeg.wasm, SQLite, Tailwind, WebSockets, nanoid, a job queue library, or any auth.

---

## Pipeline

```
game + config + seed
   → SIMULATE (pure, 120Hz fixed timestep, milliseconds, no pixels)
   → TIMELINE (keyframes every 0.5s, events, audio cues, ResultSummary)
   → RENDER (forward-only frame loop, interpolate ticks → target fps, @napi-rs/canvas)
   → ENCODE (raw RGBA piped to ffmpeg stdin; audio synthesised + mixed + muxed)
   → VERIFY (ffprobe) → output/<render-id>/video.<target>.mp4 + render.json
```

The simulation always completes before rendering starts, because the renderer needs the future: the outro card shows final standings, audio cues must land on exact frames. It runs ~1000× faster than playback, so this is invisible.

**Only one timeline is held in memory** — the current game/config/seed. Changing anything discards it and re-simulates. Option changes are debounced ~120ms and cancel any in-flight sim. Nothing accumulates; nothing writes to disk until Generate.

---

## Output

| Target | Resolution | fps |
|---|---|---|
| `vertical` | 1080×1920 | **60** |
| `vertical-30` | 1080×1920 | 30 |
| `horizontal` | 1920×1080 | **60** |

Defined in `packages/render/targets.ts`. Games declare which they support; nothing hardcodes a dimension.

**Encode:** H.264 High, CRF 18 with a per-target bitrate floor, `yuv420p`, BT.709 limited range, `-movflags +faststart`, AAC 192k/48kHz stereo, loudnorm I=−14 TP=−1.5. Constant framerate.

**Verify every render with `ffprobe`:** exact frame count, CFR, no duplicate/dropped frames. A failed check fails the render — never write a bad file.

**Output is the MP4 and nothing else.** No thumbnail, no caption file, no title/description text. `render.json` sits beside it (game, version, seed, config, duration, full `ResultSummary`) as a reproducibility receipt and the stats source. Not a deliverable.

---

## Video quality — non-negotiable

Smoothness:
- Offline frame-stepped render (rule 7). 60fps default. CFR verified.
- 120Hz sim interpolated to output rate.
- Optional motion blur per game: 4 temporal sub-samples averaged. Off by default. Never faked.

Cleanliness — **built into the primitives so an author cannot opt out:**
- All positions snap to the pixel grid. Fractional positions shimmer in motion.
- Minimum stroke 2px at 1080-wide. No 1px lines.
- Minimum text 28px at 1080-wide. Heavy weights only. Numerics in tabular figures.
- Subtle dither overlay (~1.5%, fixed per render) on large smooth gradients — prevents banding after platform recompression. *(Deferral noted 2026-10-19: the locked PEBBLE frame is a LIGHT ground with no dark areas — at Phase 3, re-scope this to whatever gradients the theme actually ships, or drop it. Until then it stays a requirement on paper only.)*
- No pure `#000000` or `#FFFFFF` in large areas. (PEBBLE's values: page mid-stop `#bab09b`, arena floor `#e7dfca`, card cream `#ede7d6`, ink `#2e2b22`.)
- Bold simple shapes over fine detail; high contrast. Fine detail dies in platform recompression.

Safe zones — enforced by `layout`, primitives refuse to draw outside:
- Vertical 1080×1920: bottom 220px, right 140px, top 160px clear.
- Horizontal 1920×1080: 5% margins.

Audio:
- Procedurally synthesised to WAV in Node, mixed from timeline cues. No copyrighted music, ever.
- −14 LUFS, true peak ≤ −1.5 dB. Every impact within ~40ms of its visual.

**Final check, always human:** watch the finished MP4 **on a phone**. Desktop browsers hide judder, shimmer, banding and illegible text.

---

## What every game shares

Decided up front, because these are the things that make ten games read as one channel — and each one is cheap to fix now and expensive to retrofit.

**Every game is a competition with a winner.** The concept is always *X versus Y*, from a head-to-head up to a multi-player free-for-all. There are no winner-less games, no pure spectacle, no ambient visuals. `ResultSummary.winnerId` and `standings` are therefore required, and the outcome panel, outro card and stats always have something to show.

**One arena, centred.** The play area is a single fixed square, the same size in every game, **centred in the frame at every aspect ratio**. 9:16 leaves more space above and below; 16:9 leaves more at the sides. The surrounding overlay — scoreboard, title, caption bars, intro, outro card — sits in that margin at fixed positions. The fixed square is the *bounds*; the playable boundary inside it is game-defined — SPINCLASH plays in a circle inscribed in the bounds. Either way, all action stays inside the bounds and compliance verifies that.

This is better than per-target layouts: one set of arena coordinates to design against, the same framing in every video, and switching aspect ratio is a pure re-encode with nothing to re-lay-out. A viewer recognises the frame before they recognise the game.

**A shared event vocabulary.** Seven core kinds the platform reacts to. Games use only the ones that apply — most will use two or three — and may add their own kinds, which the platform ignores.

**One matchup control.** A standard config helper resolves which players from the pool are competing. Every game gets the same picker, looking and behaving identically, for free.

**One default body.** `gfx.body(player, opts)` draws a player from its color, mark and name, so a game that doesn't need a bespoke look gets a consistent one for free. Games override it only where their subject genuinely demands.

**Permanent, unique colors.** Every player has a color that is theirs in every game — Speedy is green everywhere, which is what makes them recognisable. **No two players in a pool share a color**; that's a constraint on the data, checked at load, not logic resolved at runtime. All colors are distinguishable in grayscale and under deuteranopia simulation.

**Players come from data files.** A *pool* is a JSON file of players. A game declares which pool it draws from — so character games can share a recurring cast while other games define their own, and the platform never learns anyone's name. Adding a player is a data change, never code. Full model in `CONTRACT.md`.

**One skill per player per game.** Identity (name, color, mark) is global and lives in the pool. Skills are per-game and live in the game. So one player has as many skills as there are games they appear in, and each is that game's interpretation of the same idea about them.

### Naming rules

**Name a quality, not a mechanic.** A quality translates across games; a mechanic locks the player into one.

- "Heavy" is a quality — it means mass in a shoving game, area in a painting game, resistance in a timing game
- "Painter" is a mechanic — it means nothing anywhere else

**The name should let the audience predict the skill before they see it.** That's legibility for free, and legibility is the hardest thing to get in a muted video watched on a phone. "Heavy" winning a shoving match needs no explanation.

Practical constraints: names render on a scoreboard at 28px, so one or two syllables; visually distinct from each other with no near-homographs; and nothing that collides with an existing franchise.

> The roster itself — names, colors, marks, and how many — is not designed yet. Deferred to Phase 8.

### Shared vocabulary — the same words in every game

Every game on the channel uses these words with the same meaning, in docs, UI and harness output. They are platform property; no game may rename or overload them:

| Word | Means |
|---|---|
| **Player** | One participant in a match (name, color, scoreboard row). |
| **Body** | The player's on-board presence — the moving piece the audience follows. |
| **Color / tint** | The player's permanent vivid color, and its darkened text sibling. |
| **Background / ink** | The channel's ground and structural colors (paper theme). |
| **Scoreboard** | The persistent standings table listing the players and their current score or position. |
| **Banner** | A platform-injected phase or round announcement plate. |
| **Arena, pool, mark, skill, render, target, timeline, keyframe, 3-beat, safe zone** | As defined in the glossary at the end of this document. |

Game-specific mechanics get their own terms, defined once in that game's GAMES.md entry. **Synonyms are bugs:** one concept, one word, everywhere. If a word is not in this table, in the glossary below, or in a game's own GAMES.md entry, it must not appear in docs, UI or harness output.

### Game naming rules

A game's name is a channel asset: once the catalogue is bigger than one, it is what a viewer types, requests and favourites. These rules are the game-level sibling of the player naming rules above:

- **One or two words, one breath.** It must sit on the name stamp as a single plate: no punctuation, no leading "the". One word preferred; a two-word name must still sit stacked without breaking the plate, and never more than two.
- **US spelling in names.** Names use US forms (color, not colour) regardless of doc prose — search and social are the name's habitat, and they run American. Prose stays as written; a name stands as spelled.
- **Evoke the fantasy, not the ruleset.** The name says what the game feels like or what it is made of — never how it scores. Rules evolve during design; the name is forever, and the engine id (kebab-case, CONTRACT) is derived from it on day one and never changes.
- **Ownable.** Before locking, the word must not collide with an existing franchise or major title — the same check players get. Coined compounds (a material plus a verb) or real words with a double life are the cheapest way to be unique and searchable at once; the strongest names are words whose dictionary meaning *is* the game's doctrine.
- **A set, not a template.** Names should read as volumes from one press without sharing a prefix or suffix. The channel's visual system is the family resemblance; the name is the individual volume. No forced series prefix, ever.
- **Tagline: one line, six words max, present tense.** It says what the viewer watches or feels, never the scoring rule.
- **Placement.** The name appears on the outro card and in the title and description for search — **never inside the match frame** (owner decision: no game name on screen; the match is the headline). The old name-stamp concept is retired with it.

---

## House style — why ten games look like one channel

Games compose shared primitives; they don't invent their look. Raw canvas calls only for the game's unique subject matter (the track, the pieces), and only with palette colors and house easing.

**When a game needs something the design system lacks, it becomes a new platform primitive that every game gets. Never a private helper inside one game.**

Fixed across all games (the palette is the one starting direction, locked by the first game's preview):

| | |
|---|---|
| Typefaces | `Inter` (all frame type, weights 400–800; numerals tabular via `font-variant-numeric`) and `JetBrains Mono` (tooling and dev output only). The locked frame uses **no display face** — its voice is quiet print, not shout, per the preview the owner approved as the channel's look. Committed to `assets/fonts/`, loaded via `GlobalFonts.registerFromPath`. No others. |
| Palette | **Locked: PEBBLE — the paper-sheet family** (owner, 2026-10-15; reference `spinclash-preview.html` — its `TH` object and `:root` tokens). Warm gray-taupe page, light sand arena floor lighter than the page, cream cards, warm-ink + gray type, teal/amber chips. Permanent regardless: a player palette of ~24 colors, distinguishable in grayscale and under deuteranopia simulation. Each player owns one color and one text tint permanently; no two in a pool share either. |
| Motion | One easing family (fast out, soft land). Index-based stagger. No game defines its own curves. |
| Event punctuation | 3-beat — anticipation ~120ms → strike ~60ms (flash) → settle ~300ms (scoreboard/legend update). **No screen shake, no particles** — removed from the locked frame by owner decision; punctuation is flash and type only. |
| Intro, outro card, scoreboard | **Platform-injected**, including their audio cues. Games cannot skip or restyle them. |
| Arena | One fixed square, the same size in every game, **centred in the frame at every aspect ratio**. All action stays inside it; compliance verifies this. |
| Weapon art | **LANDED at build roster-r12** (2026-10-25; convention CLOSED 2026-10-27 — the prescriptive lock lives in GAMES.md, "Weapon art — the closed convention"). The practiced grammar is now prescribed by the landed art: flat fills, one uniform ink outline #2e2b22, no gradients/texture/glow; the locked paints (KW/KD/KS/KP/KB in art; KG RETIRED from art at sweep-r15, owner 2026-10-27, surviving only as the carrier-less sigil fallback) plus the sigil tag KC (carrier colour at draw), the scroll's four local reference colours, and the spell-family affinity locals (fire / poison / frost / fire-orange — owner word 2026-10-25, pre-figuring the skill pass). One diegetic sigil element per weapon (doctrine 2026-10-23, realized in the return-1 blocks); copy-kind throws draw the wielder's weapon polys at area-centroid pivots. The canonical art path is the in-file poly builder; `ingest.mjs` stands DORMANT/superseded (close item 2a). State lives in GAMES.md "Weapon art"; the 2026-10-18 locked convention and the rider-brief era are preserved in `CHRONICLE-archive.md`. |

**The paper theme — locked as PEBBLE (owner, 2026-10-15).** The channel's frame is settled: a quiet printed game sheet — warm gray-taupe page (radial `#c6bda9 → #bab09b → #aca18b`), a light warm-sand arena floor (`#e7dfca`) that always reads *lighter than the page but never glaring*, a thin mid-tone hairline rim (`#a99f86`, edge `#8d8369` — locked at rim cut two, toggle stripped), cream cards (`#ede7d6`) with warm-ink text (`#2e2b22`) and gray secondary (`#807a68`), teal chips with amber active (**preview tooling only — chips never render into a recorded frame**). The type system is three roles: **tint = who** (bot names in scorebug and legend — one reused deepened pair), **ink bold = facts** (series score, weapon names, growth stats), **gray = explanations** (skill and trait codes); cast colors set no type and appear only as fills (bots, swatches, bars). The reference implementation is `spinclash-preview.html` (its `TH` object and `:root` tokens — the picker and theme ids were stripped at lock); Phase 3 lifts the exact token table from it. Three color roles, never crossed: *color* (the player's own, permanent and vivid) for actors — bodies, bars, pills, names; *secondary gray* for explanations and numerals; *warm ink* for everything structural — lines, borders, headlines, game-defined marks. Event punctuation on the light ground: the 3-beat strike flashes ink; the hit flash is white on the struck body. The player palette requirement stands: ~24 colors, mid-lightness, high saturation on the light ground, distinguishable in grayscale and under deuteranopia simulation; each player owns one color and one tint permanently. Frame overlays follow the preview's locked frame: the **scorebug above the arena** (mini-bot discs — cast color with the bots' ink border — beside names in the players' deep tints, the series score big in ink — a plain row on the page, no container) and the **legend rows below on cream cards** — the frame's single sanctioned container, restored at the owner's request because the cards are what group each fighter's facts (deep-tint names, subtle by size; the skill and the weapon's trait as shorthand codes — `+SPD / Hit`, `+DMG / Hit`, the reveal poster also teaching the full sentences; the weapon in ink bold at the same weight as the bot names; codes and weapons stacked in a real table (auto layout aligns every column across both rows and hugs the names); growth stats as bold tabular numbers in fixed 3ch boxes, so the stats column can never grow and nothing ever reflows; no HP, which lives only on the bot bodies). The locked layout is **Columns**: one card, two rows — identity group, air, loadout group, air, stats. In-arena moments — round banners, K.O. — are type directly on the floor (SPINCLASH's K.O. card type removed at owner word 2026-10-21, "i dont want it to be announced": the round's end reads as the kill-still freeze, the faded disc and the scorebug tick; type-on-floor remains the channel rule for banners and future in-arena moments); the winner is type on the scrim. SPINCLASH's dice reveal is the owner-designed exception (2026-10-19): the VS poster covers the arena disc for its ~2.4s, then dissolves. Everywhere else the recorded frame carries no containers: emphasis is weight, size and color only. Raw cast colors set no type — actors and fills only. A game that cannot sit on this sheet (glow, neon, darkness-as-subject) is not a game for this channel. The default body is `gfx.body`; games override it only where their subject demands.

**Channel test:** render one frame from every game, tile them in a grid. They must look like one channel. Run it whenever a game is added or the design system changes.

---

## Studio

`npm run dev` → `http://127.0.0.1:5173`. Four screens. Nothing runs until the user picks a game.

1. **Games** — card per registered module: name, tagline, category, supported shapes. A broken module renders as an error card explaining itself; it must not crash the app.
2. **Setup** — left: options auto-generated from the Zod schema. Right: duration, seed field, dice, and the **outcome, visible by default** (winner, margin, lead changes, biggest comeback) — the user is a curator judging whether a render is worth publishing, not a viewer being spoiled. Below it, **per-game stats** derived on demand from `output/*/render.json`: number of renders, closest finish, biggest margin, most lead changes, biggest upset, last render. No store, no cache. Game switcher at top. One **Generate** button.
3. **Render** — progress bar, frame count, ETA, cancel. Runs in the server, so closing the tab doesn't kill it.
4. **Watch & download** — finished MP4 inline with native controls. Shape ticks (`vertical` pre-ticked) re-encode the same timeline. Download / Open output folder / Discard.

**Deliberately absent:** library screen, render history, notes, publish tracking, batch mode, preview tier, parallel renders, saved-config presets, auth. `output/` on disk is the library.

Stats are **descriptive only** — facts about renders that already happened. No leaderboards, no "best render" ranking, no charts, no suggestions about what to generate next.

---

## CLI

```bash
npm run doctor                                       # environment self-test, always first
npm run generate -- --game <id> --seed <n> --target vertical
npm run inspect  -- --game <id> --seed <n> --at 12.5 # one full-res PNG, ~200ms
npm run inspect  -- --game <id> --seed <n> --sheet   # ~24 frames tiled, ~2s
```

`doctor` checks: Node ≥22, ffmpeg resolvable, `@napi-rs/canvas` loads, fonts resolve, loopback bind works, port free, disk space. It must name the problem and the fix, not print a stack trace.

---

## Dev harness (for building games — never in the product UI)

The product loop is slow and perfect; building a game needs hundreds of fast looks.

| Tool | Cost | For |
|---|---|---|
| Single frame → PNG | ~200ms | **Colors**, layout, typography, safe zones |
| Contact sheet | ~2s | Pacing, catching a broken transition anywhere |
| Scrub view | instant | Stepping through a moment frame by frame |
| Real-time playback | instant | Motion, easing, physics feel |
| A/B (two seeds at same `t`) | ~1s | "Did that change help?" |

Scrub view and playback run the **same renderer code over the same timeline** in a browser canvas — one implementation, two backends, possible because `core` is pure and games draw against the abstract `Surface`. They capture nothing and write nothing.

Two rules: **judge color from the PNG**, not the browser (browser canvas ≠ Node Skia pixel-for-pixel). **Accept nothing until watched in the real MP4 on a phone.**

For physics-heavy games: expose physics constants in the config schema rather than hardcoding them — the auto-generated options panel becomes a tuning bench for free.

Excluded from the production build of `apps/studio`.

## Repo

```
arena-engine/
├─ SPEC.md  CONTRACT.md  BUILD.md  README.md
├─ .vscode/                  # tasks.json, launch.json, settings.json, extensions.json
├─ assets/fonts/                # Inter, JetBrains Mono (OFL), committed
├─ packages/
│  ├─ core/                  # PURE TS: contract, runtime, timeline, services, registry
│  ├─ render/                # Node only: canvas surface, frame loop, encoder, audio, targets.ts
│  └─ server/                # Fastify loopback host, single job slot
├─ apps/studio/              # Vite + React
├─ games/
│  ├─ _probe/                # throwaway contract fixtures (not content)
│  └─ _template/             # commented scaffold for a new game
├─ scripts/                  # doctor.mjs, generate.mjs, inspect.mjs
└─ output/                   # gitignored; one folder per render; also the stats source
```

Run IDs: `<game>-<YYYY-MM-DD>-<HHMMSS>`. Sortable, readable, no library.

---

## Testing

- **Determinism:** same seed twice → identical SHA-256 on the encoded file.
- **Golden frames:** committed reference PNG hash per game per version.
- **Contract compliance:** one Vitest file looping over registered games, running the eight checks in `CONTRACT.md`. Not a framework.
- **ESLint:** `no-restricted-imports` / `no-restricted-globals`, stricter for `games/` than platform code.

---

## Words used in this project

Plain terms only — broadcast jargon has been removed. These are the technical words that remain:

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Player** | One participant in a match: `id`, `name`, `color`, optional `mark`. Always a single named thing, never a crowd. Matches are 1v1 or a four-way free-for-all. (Code may use `entity` as a variable name.) |
| **Body** | The player's on-board presence — the moving piece the audience follows. `gfx.body(player, opts)` draws the default one; games override it only where their subject demands. |
| **Color** | A player's permanent, unique color — the same in every game, so they stay recognisable. No two players in a pool share one. |
| **Mark** | The detailed visual identity drawn on a player's body — a glyph for a character, a flag for a nation. Separate from color, because a flag can't fill a progress bar. |
| **Pool** | A JSON file of players, e.g. `assets/pools/characters.json`. A game declares which pool it draws from. Adding a player is a data change, never code. |
| **Scoreboard** | The persistent on-screen panel listing players and their current position or score. The thing that makes the freeze test pass. |
| **Caption bar** | A short text overlay, usually near the bottom, used for callouts. Not a subtitle file. |
| **Arena** | The one fixed square all action stays inside. Same size in every game, centred in the frame at every aspect ratio. |
| **Skill** | What makes a player behave differently. A set of optional, passive **hooks** into one game's mechanics — defined by that game, never known to the platform. Player data holds no behaviour. Exactly one skill per player per game. |
| **Frame overlay** | The fixed graphics around the arena: scoreboard, title, caption bars, intro, outro. Platform-injected; games can't restyle them. |
| **Intro / outro** | The short branded opening and the result card at the end. Same in every video. |
| **3-beat** | How a significant moment is punctuated: anticipation (~120ms) → strike (~60ms, flash) → settle (~300ms, scoreboard update). No shake, no particles — the locked frame punctuates with light and type only. |
| **Timeline** | The recorded result of a completed simulation: keyframes, events, audio cues, result summary. The renderer walks it to produce frames. |
| **Keyframe** | A full snapshot of the simulation every 0.5s, so the renderer can re-enter the timeline cheaply. |
| **Render** *(noun)* | One generation, from pressing Generate to an MP4. Identified by `<game>-<date>-<time>`. Avoid "run" for this — in a racing game a *run* means an attempt down the track, and the collision is endless confusion. |
| **Target** | An export preset: `vertical`, `vertical-30`, `horizontal`. |
| **CFR** | Constant frame rate. Every frame occupies exactly the same duration; verified with `ffprobe` on every render. |
| **Dither overlay** | Faint fixed noise over dark backgrounds. Stops them banding after a platform recompresses the video. |
| **Safe zone** | Screen edges kept clear because platform UI covers them (bottom 220px, right 140px, top 160px on vertical). |
| **Probe** | A throwaway game used to validate the contract. Not content, never published. |

---

## Deferred on purpose

Settled as "decide later," with the phase where each gets decided:

| | When | Why wait |
|---|---|---|
| **The games** — mechanics, arenas, pacing | Phase 8 | Designing them before any frame has been rendered is guessing |
| **Players and pools** — the roster: names, colors, marks, how many | Phase 8 | Depends on the games. The *mechanism* is settled (CONTRACT.md §Skills); the cast is not |
| **Concrete visual identity** — engine token table, type scale, scoreboard layout, the designed intro and outro | Phase 3 | Theme **locked** (PEBBLE, paper-sheet family, owner 2026-10-15); what remains is the engineered token set lifted from `spinclash-preview.html`, the type scale and the designed intro/outro |
| **Audio identity** — the sound palette, what a match's turning points and its ending sound like, whether there's a musical signature | Phase 3 | Same. Technical requirements are locked; the sounds are not |
| **Non-Latin scripts, long player names** | When pools exist | Nations were an example, not a commitment |
| **Standard config fields** — player count, duration, match structure | After the second game | One game can't reveal what's common |
| **Sound-effect vocabulary** — the set of names games call via `sfx()` | After the second game | Same |
| **Match structure and escalation** — whether a platform-level tension system is worth having | After the second game | Games may simply be designed to have shape; don't build a system to compensate for flat mechanics |

**Settled since this table was written:** skills are per-game hooks with no platform-level system (see `CONTRACT.md`), which resolved the "signature moves" and "escalation ownership" questions.

**The rule for the remaining ones:** the first game is built freely, with no attempt to generalise. When the second game is designed, whatever the two share gets extracted and promoted into the platform. Extracting a standard from two real examples beats inventing one upfront — and inventing one upfront is how a platform accumulates abstractions nothing uses.

None of these block Phases 0–2. The pipeline, the contract and the compliance suite need no palette, no sounds and no characters.

---

## Scope

Out, permanently or until v1 ships: content strategy, game design, publishing/upload tooling, accounts, analytics, non-loopback networking, telemetry, 3D/WebGL, LLM calls, UI-based game authoring, plugins, desktop packaging, i18n, mobile.

The tool never touches publishing or revenue. What it *does* own is every technical property that decides whether a video is eligible and competitive: resolution, framerate, codec, loudness, safe zones, legibility, house style.

---

## Prior art

Two architectural patterns here — behaviour as optional passive hooks defined locally by each game, and a single fixed arena centred at every aspect ratio — were inspired by an existing open animation-engine project.

**No text, code, template, character, or game design was copied from it.** Both patterns are described above in our own terms and are adapted to an offline render pipeline that project does not have. The games, players and visual identity in this project are entirely our own.

The owner contacted that project's owners and received **explicit permission for any use, including commercial**. We chose original designs regardless: their specific ruleset, text and code were not copied.
